title: Part 2: Cue Card — What Happens and What's Expected
blocks: At the end of Part 1, the examiner will say something like this: "Now I'm going to give you a topic, and I'd like you to talk about it for one to two minutes. Before you talk, you'll have one minute to think about what you're going to say. You can make some notes if you wish." Then they will give you a card, a piece of paper and a pencil. The card looks like this:

**Describe a skill you learned from an older person.**
You should say:

  what the skill is

  who taught you and when

  how you learned it

and explain how you feel about having this skill now.

Every card has the same structure: a **main topic** (the first line), three **bullet points** (hints about what to say), and at the end an **"and explain..."** — which always asks for your feelings, opinion or reasons. This last line is the most important and the most often ignored.
What the examiner is looking for here

Part 2 is the only part of the test where you speak **alone, continuously and without interruption**. In Part 1, the short questions help you; in Part 3, the examiner's questions give you direction. In Part 2, the direction is up to you. So here the examiner mainly looks at:
Can you keep talking for **up to 2 minutes**, or do you run out after 45 seconds?
Is your talk **going somewhere** — does it have a beginning, a middle and an end — or is it all over the place?
Can you **tell a story** — past tense, sequence, description, feelings?
Are you staying **on the topic**, or saying something else (something memorised)?
**Try to fill the full 2 minutes.** The examiner will stop you at 2 minutes — that's a good sign. If you stop before 1 minute, it directly hurts your FC score.
**Don't be upset if you're stopped.** "...and that's when I— " "Thank you." — that's the script. Being stopped midway means you had plenty to say.

**Use the full time for your 1-minute notes.** There's no benefit in saying "I'm ready" and starting early — in fact, it hurts you. 60 seconds of thinking now means 60 seconds less thinking during your 2-minute talk.

title: The 1-Minute Note: What to Write and What Not to Write
blocks: The biggest mistake in note-taking is **writing sentences**. In one minute you can write two sentences at most, and then you'll read those two sentences out — reading, not speaking. The examiner can tell the difference between reading and speaking in a second.
The second mistake is **writing nothing at all** — "I can keep it in my head". 90 seconds in, feeling nervous, you'll forget your third point.

Write **one keyword** for each of the card's four lines (three bullets + "explain"), plus **one extra** — something the card didn't ask for but that makes your story real. That's 5 words in total, in capital letters, written one below the other. For the card above, it could be:

SEWING — grandmother, Eid holidays, age 12

WATCH → PRACTISE → MISTAKES (crooked hem)

NOW: fix own clothes, save money

FEEL: proud, connected to her

+ old black machine, foot pedal sound

Notice: each line can be read at a glance, and you can get 2-3 sentences out of each word. The last line (+) is the "sensory detail" — a sight, sound or smell that makes the story feel true and gives you a chance to show your vocabulary.
Read the whole card — especially the last line. Choose **one** specific thing/person/event. Don't hesitate between two; take the first one that comes to mind, the one you have more to say about.
Say your first sentence in your head. If the start is right, the rest follows.

**Being truthful about the topic:** "Describe a skill you learned from an older person" — if you don't really have anything like this, make it up, or use something close (even if you learned it from a friend, say "my older cousin"). The examiner doesn't check whether it's true. But **don't change the topic** — talking about a journey instead of a skill is off-topic, and it hurts your FC score.

title: The 2-Minute Talk: Structure
blocks: This is Tip #3 — "Master Part 2 Structure". Any cue card, any topic: the same five steps. This is the only thing in this book you need to memorise — and once you've memorised it, you don't need to memorise anything else.
What you're going to talk about — in one sentence, paraphrasing the card's wording.
I'd like to talk about... / The [skill/place/person] I've chosen is... / OK, so this is about...
What, who, when, where — the background. Past tense here, and description of the person/place.
This was back when... / It all started... / She was the kind of person who...
How — step by step, a small incident, a problem and its solution. This is where the story is.
At first... then... / The tricky part was... / I remember one time...
The last line of the card. How you feel, why it matters, what has changed. Come back to the present tense.
Looking back, ... / What it means to me now is... / The reason it matters is...
Finish in one sentence — the future, or the main point again.
So, all in all... / That's why I'll always... / I suppose that's the story of...
Worked example: from note to talk
The full talk built from the note above. Each step is marked. It's about 2 minutes — 280-300 words at a natural pace.

**[1 Opening]** The skill I'd like to talk about is sewing, which I learned from my grandmother when I was about twelve.
**[2 Context]** This was during the long Eid holidays, when we'd go to stay at her house in the village for a couple of weeks. She had this ancient black sewing machine — the kind you work with a foot pedal — and I can still hear the rhythm of it, this steady clacking sound coming from the back room every afternoon. She was a very patient woman, but also quite strict about doing things properly, which turned out to be exactly what I needed.
**[3 Process]** At first she wouldn't let me touch the machine at all. For the first few days I just watched her, and then she gave me scraps of old cloth to practise straight lines on. The tricky part was keeping the pressure on the pedal steady — I remember my first hem came out completely crooked, and instead of fixing it for me, she made me unpick the whole thing and do it again. I was annoyed at the time, but by the end of the holiday I'd made a small cushion cover on my own.
**[4 Explain]** Looking back, I feel genuinely proud of having this skill, partly because so few people my age can do it. On a practical level, I fix my own clothes instead of throwing them away, which saves money and, honestly, feels quite satisfying. But more than that, every time I sit at a machine I feel connected to her — she passed away a few years ago, and this is the most tangible thing she left me.
**[5 Closing]** So I suppose it's much more than a skill to me; it's a bit of her that I still carry around.

What this talk contains that the examiner is looking for: past narrative (was, wouldn't let, came out, made me), sensory detail (black machine, clacking sound), a small problem and its solution (crooked hem), reflection in the present tense, precise vocabulary (ancient, steady, unpick, tangible), and a clear ending.

title: Strategies for Filling 2 Minutes
blocks: "I have nothing to say" — this is the most common complaint about Part 2, and it's almost always wrong. There are things to say; you just don't know which angle to look from. Apply the 6 "lenses" below to any topic, and 2 minutes will actually feel short.
When was the first time? What's it like now? What comes next?
First went there in 2nd year... now go every Thursday... will probably keep going after I graduate.
What does it look, sound, smell and taste like?
Dim yellow lights, smell of cardamom tea, old Bangla songs playing softly.
Who is there? Who do you go with?
The owner, who remembers everyone's order; my two closest friends.
How is it different from the others? What was there before?
Unlike the chain cafés, nobody hurries you out; before it opened, there was nowhere to sit near campus.
A small incident on one particular day?
The night we stayed until closing finishing a group project, and the owner brought us free tea.
What does it mean in your life? What has it changed?
It's where most of my university friendships were actually built.
The card's three bullets usually cover lenses 1, 3 and 5; the "explain" line is lens 6. The other two (senses, contrast) are your own additions — and they are what turn a Band 6 into a Band 7.
If you run out of things to say midway
**Look at your notes** — which keyword haven't you used yet? Go there: "Oh, and another thing I should mention is..."
**Switch lenses**: you've been describing what happened → now say how you feel about it. "Thinking about it now, ..."
**Make a comparison**: "Compared to other [cafés/gifts/journeys] I've had, this one..."
**Wrap it up** — once you've passed 1 minute 20 seconds, stopping neatly with a closing is better than forcing it to drag on.
The language of Part 2: a storytelling toolkit
back in [year], a few years ago, when I was in my final year, at the time, around that period, it must have been [season]
to begin with, after a while, the next thing I knew, eventually, by the end of it, in the end
she was the kind of person who..., he had a way of..., what struck me about her was..., a bit of a [perfectionist / joker]
tucked away behind..., it's the sort of place where..., what makes it special is..., nothing fancy, but...
I was over the moon, I was a nervous wreck, I couldn't believe my luck, I was a bit taken aback, it was a real eye-opener
looking back, in hindsight, thinking about it now, it still makes me smile, I'll always be grateful for
the thing I remember most vividly is..., what really stood out was..., I'll never forget...
Going through the card's bullets one by one with one sentence each ("The skill is sewing. My grandmother taught me. I learned by practising. I feel good.") — finished in 30 seconds.
Think of each bullet as a paragraph of 2-4 sentences. Use the lenses.
Speaking in general terms ("Sewing is a useful skill. Many people learn sewing...") — that's Part 3 language.
Part 2 is personal and specific: "I", "my", a particular person, day or place.
Giving a memorised talk that only partly matches the card.
The examiner will notice and ask different questions in the follow-up. Memorise the structure, not the content.
Using the present tense in a story about the past ("Then she gives me cloth and I practise...").
Write "PAST" next to your notes. If you start your first sentence in the past, the rest is easier.
Giving the whole talk while looking at your notes.
Notes are for a quick glance; 80% of the time, look at the examiner.
Leaving out the "Explain" line, or getting it over with in one sentence.
This is the 30-second part, and it's where the best vocabulary (feelings, reflection) comes in.

At the end of your talk, the examiner may ask one or two short questions: "Do you still sew?", "Would you teach this to someone?" These are not Part 3 — answer in **one or two sentences**. If you give a long answer, they will stop you.

title: Part 3: Discussion — The Game Changes
blocks: At the end of Part 2, the examiner takes the card back and says: "We've been talking about a skill you learned from an older person, and I'd like to discuss with you one or two more general questions related to this." Those words "more general" are what Part 3 is all about. The questions are no longer about you — they're about **people, society, the country and the future**.
Describe a skill you learned from an older person.

What kinds of skills do older people typically pass on to younger generations? / Are traditional skills disappearing in your country? Why? / Should schools teach practical skills like cooking or repairing things? / In the future, will people learn more from other people or from the internet?

This is Tip #5 — "Handle Part 3 Abstract Questions". In Part 3, the examiner wants to see whether you can **give opinions, explain reasons, compare, speculate and see both sides** — in other words, whether you can **think** in English. This is your biggest chance to show your range of vocabulary and grammar, and most Band 7 decisions are made here.
**"I have to give the right answer."** No. The examiner has no answer key. Whatever opinion you can explain best is the right one.

**"I have to know about the subject."** No. "I don't know much about this, but I'd guess..." — this is a perfectly acceptable start; then make a reasoned guess. Your language is assessed, not your knowledge.
**"Short answers, like in Part 1."** No. Part 3 answers are 4-6 sentences, 30-45 seconds. The examiner will stop you if they want to; don't stop on your own after two sentences.

title: 8 Types of Part 3 Questions
blocks: Like Part 2, Part 3 is predictable — not the topics, but the **question types**. Whatever the topic, the examiner asks these 8 types of question. If you can recognise each one, the language for your answer is already prepared.
Do you think...? Should...? Is it better to...?
I'd say / I tend to think / I'm inclined to believe / on balance
Why do people...? What makes...? Why is ... popular?
the main reason is / it's largely because / one factor is / this is partly down to
What effect does ... have on...? How does ... influence...?
this leads to / as a result / one consequence is / it tends to make people
How is ... different from...? Old vs young? City vs village?
whereas / while / unlike / on the one hand... on the other / far more likely to
Has ... changed? How was it different in the past?
used to / these days / there's been a shift towards / a generation ago
Will ... in the future? How might ... change?
I imagine / it's likely that / we may well see / I doubt whether / in the next decade or so
How can we...? What should the government do?
one option would be / the government could / a more effective approach might be / it would help if
Advantages/disadvantages? Is it a good thing?
the upside is / a major drawback / it cuts both ways / the benefits outweigh

title: A.R.E + Balance: The Framework for Part 3
blocks: The A.R.E from Parts A and B works here too — just with a fourth step added. In Part 3, the examiner wants to see whether you can see **more than one side** of an issue. So end your answer with a "but" — the other side, a condition, or an exception.

**A.R.E + B**
**A — Answer:** a clear opinion, in the first sentence. (A little more hedged than in Part 1: "I'd say", "generally")

**R — Reason:** why — one or two reasons, talking about people/society in general.

**E — Example:** a concrete example — your own country, someone you know, a trend.

**B — Balance:** "Having said that..." / "Of course, it depends..." / "That's not to say..." — the other side, in one or two sentences.

**Q:** Should schools teach practical skills like cooking or repairing things?
**A:** I think they should, yes — at least the basics.
**R:** The main reason is that these are skills everyone needs, regardless of what career they end up in, and a lot of families simply don't pass them on anymore because parents are working long hours.
**E:** In my country, for instance, plenty of university students can solve calculus problems but can't cook a meal or change a fuse, and they end up either dependent on others or spending money they don't have.
**B:** Having said that, I wouldn't want it to eat into academic time — maybe an hour a week would be enough, rather than a whole subject.

With these four steps, you show all of this in a single answer: opinion language, cause language, an example (a chance for LR), and contrast (GRA — 'although', 'whereas', conditional). That's a Band 7 Part 3 answer.
Having said that, / Then again, / That said, / Mind you, / On the flip side,
It really depends on..., / As long as..., / Provided that..., / Unless...
That's not to say..., / Of course, there are exceptions — / This doesn't apply to everyone;
To some extent, / Up to a point, / In most cases, though not all,
I think the answer is somewhere in the middle. / It's probably a case of both. / The ideal would be a mix of...
Hedging: polite language for giving opinions

In Part 3, saying something like "Governments must ban cars" sounds immature. "I think governments should probably look at restricting cars in city centres" — the same opinion, but in the language of a thoughtful person. This hedging is essential for Band 7+:
People tend to be less active than they used to be.
It's quite likely to happen. / I'd expect that to happen.
Most people would probably agree that... / There's a general feeling that...
This can be problematic in some ways. / I'm not sure this is entirely a good thing.
The internet is arguably one of the main reasons. / I'd put a lot of it down to the internet.
When you don't know the answer
In Part 3 you will definitely get questions you've never thought about. When that happens, there are three routes — all acceptable; silence is not:
**Think and speculate:** "That's not something I've thought about, but I'd imagine... because..."
**Generalise from your own experience:** "I can only really speak from what I've seen in my own family, but there..."
**Narrow the question down:** "It probably depends a lot on the country. In mine, ..."
You can't just say "I don't know" to the examiner and stop — but you can say "I don't know, but..." and keep going.

title: Worked Example: A Full Part 3 on One Topic
blocks: Below is a full Part 3 arising from a Part 2 topic — 6 of the 8 question types, each answered with A.R.E + B. Notice the length of the answers: 4-6 sentences.
**The Part 2 topic was: Describe a journey you took by public transport that you remember well.**

Q1 (Reason): Why do some people prefer public transport to driving?
A: I'd say it comes down to cost and stress, mostly. Owning a car is enormously expensive once you add fuel, parking and repairs, whereas a bus or metro pass is a fraction of that. On top of that, in a congested city, sitting on a train reading is far less draining than sitting in traffic gripping a steering wheel. My cousin actually sold his car last year for exactly that reason. Of course, this only holds where public transport is decent — if the buses are unreliable, people will drive no matter the cost.
Q2 (Compare): How is travelling by public transport different in cities and in the countryside?
A: They're almost two different worlds. In cities, the issue is usually overcrowding — the transport exists, but there's too much demand for it, so rush hour is unpleasant. In rural areas, it's the opposite: services are so infrequent that missing one bus can mean waiting three hours. Where my grandparents live, there are two buses a day, so people plan their whole week around them. Having said that, rural journeys tend to be more pleasant when they do happen — you actually get a seat and a view.
Q3 (Past vs Now): Has public transport in your country changed in recent years?
A: Quite dramatically, at least in the capital. A generation ago it was entirely buses — old, crowded, with no fixed timetable. Now there's a metro line, and it's changed people's expectations: for the first time, a journey has a predictable length. That said, outside the capital things have moved much more slowly, so the gap between the big city and everywhere else has, if anything, widened.
Q4 (Solution): What could governments do to encourage more people to use public transport?
A: The most effective thing would probably be reliability rather than price. People will pay a reasonable fare if they know the bus will actually come. So investing in proper timetables, dedicated bus lanes and real-time tracking apps would do more than subsidies. Singapore is often cited as an example where this works. I'd add, though, that carrots alone aren't enough — some cities have only succeeded when they also made driving less convenient, through congestion charges or parking limits.
Q5 (Evaluate): What are the disadvantages of relying on public transport?
A: The obvious one is loss of control — you're tied to someone else's schedule and route, which is a real problem if you work irregular hours or have young children to carry around. There's also the comfort issue; a packed bus in forty-degree heat is nobody's idea of a good start to the day. And for people with mobility problems, a lot of systems simply aren't accessible. On balance, though, I'd argue these are problems of poor implementation rather than of public transport itself.
Q6 (Predict): How do you think people will travel around cities in fifty years?
A: I'd imagine private car ownership will have dropped sharply, at least in cities. Between shared electric vehicles, better rail and possibly self-driving shuttles, owning a car that sits parked ninety percent of the time will seem wasteful, the way owning a landline seems now. I'm less sure about the timeline — these things always take longer than the headlines suggest. And I doubt it'll happen evenly; wealthier cities will get there first, and places like mine might still be catching up.
Talking about yourself as in Part 1 ("I use the bus every day because...") when the question is about people in general.
Start with "People", "most families", "in my country"; use your own example only in the E step.
A.R.E + B — don't stop until you've gone through all four steps.
Only one opinion, only one side.
The Balance step is compulsory — it's where you show complex grammar.
Wasting time with "It's a good question", and then still giving an introduction.
One filler phrase, then straight to A.
Collapsing under the examiner's counter-argument (changing your opinion when you hear "But some people say...").
The examiner is testing whether you can hold your opinion. "That's a fair point, but I'd still say..." — keep your opinion and expand your language.

title: How to Practise Parts 2 and 3
blocks: **One cue card a day** (from Part D). 1 minute of notes — timer on your phone. 2 minutes of talk — recorded.
**Three questions when you listen to the recording:** Did you reach 2 minutes? Were all five steps there? Was your past tense correct?
**The Part 3 questions for the same card** (given with each card in Part D) — answer each one with A.R.E + B, 30-45 seconds.
**One full mock a week:** a friend or family member plays the examiner — Part 1 to Part 3, 12 minutes, recorded.
**After four weeks, listen to your first week's recording.** You'll hear the difference yourself — and that will be your source of confidence on test day.

title: The Week Before the Test: Checklist
blocks: The book is finished. Now come the last seven days of turning it into a score.
Reread the "10 Speaking Tips" in Part A. Listen to your oldest recording, then your newest — hear the difference. That is your confidence.
Part B: 10 random topics, 2 questions on each, using the three strategies. Record yourself and just count the 'umm's.
4 cue cards from Part D, from four different categories, timed. Answer each card's Part 3 questions with A.R.E + B.
Full mock: a friend as examiner, 12 minutes, Part 1→3, recorded. Listen back and compare yourself with the band descriptors in Part A.
Pronunciation day: pairs of difficult sounds, 10 minutes of shadowing, and one Part 2 talk purely for stress and intonation.
Second full mock, on different topics. Read the "10 mistakes Bangla speakers make" list in Part A out loud once.
**Nothing new.** Read the "Test day" chapter in Part A. Sort out your ID, the test centre address and your clothes. Have a relaxed 15-minute chat with someone in English. Go to bed early.

From one hour before, English only. Take three deep breaths before you enter the room. Make your first sentence clear, and say it with a smile. If you pause in an answer, pause in English. At the end, "Thank you". You know the rest.

**Final word:** The examiner is not against you. They are sitting there to hear you speak English for 11 minutes, and their job is to find out what you can do. Your job is simply to let them hear it. This book is here to make that easier. The rest — the preparation you have done — is yours.
